title: Va'era: too tired to hear (Exodus 6:9)
hookLine: the people can't listen "for impatience of spirit, and for cruel bondage"
tomorrow: Va'era: why Aaron struck the river

cards: You come home with great news: a better apartment, a plan to fix the money problem, a way out of the thing that's been dragging everyone down.
And the person you tell has just worked a double shift, the baby was up all night, and they barely look up. You say it again. Nothing.
It's not that they don't care. They can't take it in. Moses has the news they've been waiting for: God has promised freedom, four times over.
He tells the people. And they don't listen.

teach.b: The verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "but they hearkened not unto Moses for impatience of spirit, and for cruel bondage." The Hebrew for impatience of spirit is kotzer ruach.
Literally, shortness of spirit, or shortness of breath; ruach is both. Rashi pictures it physically: a person in distress whose breath comes short, who can't draw a long breath.
That's how breathing goes when someone is panicked or exhausted: quick, shallow, high in the chest. There's no room in there for a new idea. And notice what the Torah doesn't do.
It doesn't call the people faithless or stubborn. It gives the reason right there in the verse: cruel bondage, hard labor.
They're too crushed to hope, and the text takes their side. Then Moses, discouraged, turns it on himself: if my own people won't listen to me, how will Pharaoh?

teach.h: GO BACK AND SAY IT AGAIN.
teach.b: God's answer is simply to send him back, with Aaron, to both. Again. Later, when the people are free, they do hear.
At the sea, the Torah says, they believed.
Freedom came first. Listening came after.
So when someone can't hear good news, or advice, or even love, the verse invites a different question. Not, why won't they listen? But, how short is their breath right now?
What are they carrying? Sometimes the first job isn't to say it better. It's to lighten the load, and wait.

how: Some Jewish teachers read kotzer ruach as a lesson about burnout and hardship, and the Torah itself commands paying a hired worker's wages the same day and giving servants and laborers the Sabbath rest.

o: short breath, Rashi's picture of a person in distress
and I appeared, God's words that open the portion
and he heard, the people taking in Moses's news

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: a person whose breath comes short

s: the Torah blames the people for not listening
it gives the reason in the same verse: shortness of spirit and cruel bondage.
ruach can mean both spirit and breath
so kotzer ruach is shortness of spirit and shortness of breath.
God gave up on the people when they wouldn't listen
God sent Moses and Aaron back to speak again.

games.q: you're Moses. you brought the people God's promise of freedom, and they were too crushed to listen. what now?
o: wait until they come to you.
games.why: Moses was discouraged, but God sent him back, with Aaron, to the people and to Pharaoh. later, at the sea, the people believed.

practice: Notice your own breath, and if it's short, let it lengthen, slowly, a few times.
Then think of someone who hasn't been hearing you lately, a partner, a parent, a coworker, a teenager, and ask what their bondage is right now, what hard labor they're under.
Picture one way to lighten it before you try to be heard.

wordCard.voice: Va'era. The portion where the people can't hear Moses's good news, for shortness of spirit and cruel bondage.

orig.note: Hebrew: shortness of spirit, shortness of breath (Exodus 6:9).
